## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Patrol officers and deputies who write incident reports from body-cam footage.
   [LYC] "Intros to Police, Sheriff, Transit, or University PDs that wrestle with video or paperwork overload."
   [LYC] "We auto-generate reports, verify narratives, and surface evidence instantly — cutting desk time by 60% and
   putting officers where communities need them most." → `roles[officer]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.
   Author's choice: "at small and mid-sized police departments" stands for [LYC]'s "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers)".

2. **What (the job).** Get every call written up as a report, accurately, without the officer stuck at the desk.
   [LYC] "40% of a typical shift vanishes to transcribing body-cam footage, filling forms, and locating clips across
   siloed systems." [YCW] "Officers spend up to a third of their shifts manually transcribing body camera footage".
   → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** After a call, when the footage has to become a report; at the desk, often past end of shift.
   [PR] (Chief Sever) "an officer might not be as detailed if they're 'down 10 reports'". [PR] "End-of-shift reports,
   which provide an overview of incidents over an entire shift, will continue to be written exclusively by humans."
   → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: incident report`. Author's choice: the window {7, DAYS} (spec 120: "every shift"
   reads as 7 DAYS) and Frequency 3 to 5 days out of 7 (an officer works about four or five shifts in seven; the posts
   say "a typical shift", so every shift worked). Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "a typical shift".

4. **Which people.** US police, sheriff, transit and university departments of 10 to 200 officers.
   [LYC] "Design-partner agencies (10–200 officers) willing to co-shape features." [LYC] "We'll fly anywhere in North
   America to set you up within 48 hours—no strings attached." → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The department, per officer a month; the chief decides under a spending cap, the city council above it.
   [PR] "Sever said he's only able to authorize expenditures up to a certain amount without Heber City Council approval.
   Purchasing Draft One for around $30,000 per year would require such permission. Buying Code Four at around $6,000 to
   $8,000 per year would not." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: chief}`; Buyer and payer tests "Nobody else" (the
   chief alone), with "The city council" and "The city manager" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A side-by-side
   trial against Axon's tool", is from [PR] ("The Police Department recently completed free trial periods of two AI
   programs") and [CMP] ("We ran 30 days with Axon Draft One and 30 days with Code Four... 17/18 Officers chose Code Four
   at the end of the trial."); the other two items (a records-system check; the prosecutor's office agreeing) are the
   author's, the second from [BDN] (the district attorney: "It's not something that my office, or our PDs, have agreed
   is ready for use."). Commitment's step, "run a free pilot with a few officers": [LYC] "no strings attached"; [BDN]
   "he has provided a year of the software for free"; [PR] the free trial periods. Header: the outside payer (gap 2).

6. **Mechanism.** Footage in; a draft narrative in the department's format, each fact tied to its clip, with check
   words the officer must remove.
   [LYC] "Autofilled narrative reports that match your RMS schema and chain-of-custody rules." [LYC] "Real-time
   transcription & summarization — every body-cam or interview video becomes searchable text + key-frame timelined."
   [LYC] "One-click redaction — faces, plates, minors' voices, and PII are masked with CJIS-compliant logs."
   [BDN] (Cheng) "Essentially, we make it so that the patrol is reviewing the reports rather than writing the reports
   from scratch"; "Code Four inserts extraneous, random or incorrect information into the reports. If an officer doesn't
   remove that information, they cannot submit a final draft." [CMP] "Every report fact links to the source clip,
   transcript, and timestamp". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility (footage uploaded before
   the shift ends — tested; typed into the records system; time to read a draft) and Adoption friction (read and
   correct every draft — tested; delete the check words). Relative advantage's two benefits: [LYC] "cutting desk time
   by 60%" (shorter_time) and [CMP] "Code Four analyzes every frame of body camera footage, not just the audio"
   (less_worry); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** $30 per officer a month; the cost is the officers' report time.
   [BI] "Cheng said Code Four works with 25 police departments and makes money via a subscription model, which starts
   at $30 per officer a month." [PR] "Code Four is significantly cheaper at $30 per officer per month. Sever estimated it
   would cost Heber City between $6,000 and $8,000 annually." → `commercial.price` AMOUNT_PERIOD $30 to $30 per officer
   (the cost's unit and month).
   Existing sacrifice, HOURS 40 to 60 of the incident reports per officer a month: author's arithmetic from [YCW] "up
   to a third of their shifts" and [LYC] "40% of a typical shift", on 8-to-10-hour shifts and about fifteen shifts a
   month (a third of 8 hours x 15 = 40; 40% of 10 hours x 15 = 60). The rate, $37 an hour, is [BLS] "The median annual
   wage for police and detectives was $77,310 in May 2025" ($37.17 an hour), the author's stand-in: no source gives an
   officer's hour. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (hours never compare with dollars).

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these public accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [PR] (a Heber City sergeant, of a report drafted with an AI tool) "This report would have taken me an hour, and it
   took me eight minutes." [CMP] (a chief, vendor-curated) "Code Four helped one of my guys who was 3 weeks behind
   reports finish his reports" (the quote goes on; its last words are not reproduced here). [BDN] (a researcher) "There's
   a lot of error there because of background noise: being on the side of a highway, of trucks driving by".

## Status today

Widened, same core. [SITE] today sells four products (report writing, investigations over phone dumps and jail calls,
redaction, a mobile field-capture app) and claims "Live in 200+ departments"; [YCP] reads "Modernizing the police
workflow." Customer counts in the press: 25 departments ([BI] 2025-11-19), about 50 ([BDN] 2026-02-24). Price today:
no public price list ([SITE], read 2026-10-22); the latest dated figure is [BDN] "If the department decides to continue
using it, they will pay $50 per officer per month, or about $3,000 to $5,000 a year for the small department." (after a
free first year).

## Could not be sourced

- **A launch-era price.** Neither [LYC] nor the site's archived snapshot of 2025-07-01 carries one; the earliest dated
  price is [BI]'s $30 per officer a month, six months after launch. It is used as the founder's price because it is the
  nearest dated figure and the price the company named publicly first; a reader holding the entry to the launch era
  should treat the price as one step later than the rest.
- **An officer's hour.** No source gives one; [BLS]'s median for police and detectives stands in.
- **The hours per officer a month.** The founders give shares of a shift, not hours; the 40 to 60 is the author's
  arithmetic (item 7).
- **A buyer title for the cap.** Only Heber City's chief is on record ([PR]); that every chief has a cap, and that the
  council and city manager are the other roles, is the author's reading.
- **A Launch HN thread or first-person officer accounts.** None exists; officer occasions are scripted from [PR], [BDN]
  and [CMP] (the last vendor-curated).
- The footage-upload condition (tested Compatibility), the three Purchase friction items but the trial, and every pick
  are the author's.

screens.why4: The five rows run cleanly from on time to never, they don't overlap, and they cover the real answers, including the officer who is weeks behind.
screens.why5: My claim is that report-writing eats the shift, but this scale only measures lateness, so it drifted a little; the bar also names 'Finished at the desk before end of shift' in one place and 'Finished it later the same shift' in another, and the first isn't a row at all.
screens.instead: Keep the five rows, and set the bar to hold if at least 2 in 3 land below 'Finished the report right after the call', since a report that waits for desk time later in the shift is already the time we take off patrol.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, and as the founder I can see why Keel asks it now.
screens.why2: The question and hint are clear, but 'Lock and record the face Keel preselects' made me read it twice to work out whether I'm choosing a face, recording myself, or accepting a default.
screens.why3: I know the officers I'm sending this to and can judge whether an AI face or a typed screen will get a cop to answer a text from a stranger.
screens.why4: The picked option is worded around Keel's mechanics ('lock and record') rather than what I'd want, so it doesn't sit cleanly beside a plain 'use Keel's interviewer' or 'record my own face' choice.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes my context or leaks Code Four or my roles to the officers; it only sets who delivers the questions.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? — Keel's AI interviewer (pick a face) / Me, on a short recorded video / No video, written questions only

screens.why1: Right after picking who asks the questions, it is obvious to decide how my patrol officers will answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the doubled 'Daphne Daphne' and the bare tags 'Hear her' and 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' read like screen leftovers and take a second read to work out that her video isn't made yet.
screens.why3: I know my officers answer on a phone between calls, often in a cruiser or on a loud roadside, so I can judge text versus a talking interviewer from what I know of their shifts.
screens.why4: Talk, read-and-tap, or let them choose covers it with no overlap, and the noise figure for Daphne matters for officers on a highway shoulder.
screens.why5: It keeps 'patrol officers' as I typed it and shows nothing of my product to the officer.
screens.instead: How should patrol officers answer? — Daphne, an AI interviewer, asks aloud on video (her video is still being made, ready in a few minutes) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose (ready once Daphne is)

screens.why1: Right after choosing how officers answer, the last step is who receives the interview, so it is obvious why it closes the flow.
screens.why2: Each choice says plainly how the link goes out, whether to people I know, a Keel list or one open link, and I can pick on first read.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching officers through named intros from our design-partner agencies or through an open post, so this is my own decision to make.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and cover how I would reach officers, and 'People I know by name' fits my intros to 10-to-200-officer departments.
screens.why5: Nothing here alters the study I typed, and nothing of Code Four's product reaches the officers through this choice.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside 'Frequency: 4 answered', but the line names only Frequency when three of my four cards are short, and it doesn't say 5 were needed until I reach the cards.
screens.why_b2: Prevalence's '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar' reads at once, but 7 officers answered and only 4 count on the other three cards, and nothing here says why the other 3 dropped out.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution carry the belief lines I checked on the way in word for word, and Prevalence and Frequency are my 8-in-10 and 3-to-5-days-of-7 claims.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers but never says it, for example 'one more officer's answer on Frequency, Importance and Current solution decides them', so I have to work out the next step myself.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and the low counts are called 'too few', but a verdict line naming only Frequency softly suggests Importance and Current solution are settled when they are just as uncounted.
screens.instead: Too few to call: Frequency, Importance and Current solution each counted 4 of the 7 officers (3 didn't reach those questions) and need 5. Get one or two more officers to answer before reading them. Prevalence holds, but only just, at 6 of 7 against a bar of 6.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows one cell per officer, 6 for me and 1 against, on a 0-to-7 axis with my bar marked at 6, so I can see what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits at first look.
screens.why_b3: I said reports eat 40% of a typical shift, and 'fell behind on their call reports' is Keel's rewording of that, still recognisable as my belief, but 'the most recent time it happened' after a yes/no question reads like a stray fragment.
screens.why_b4: 'Common among these 7, at your bar exactly' plus a pointer to the next two cards tells me to keep reading, but it says nothing concrete for the idea, such as that one more 'no' would sink it, so a bigger sample is needed before I quote it to chiefs.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' and 'at your bar exactly' keep 'Holding up' from sounding stronger than 6 of 7 can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 officers fell behind on reports this week, exactly my bar, so one more 'no' would flip it. Treat it as a lean and widen the sample before leaning on it in a pitch.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted, 5 needed', and the strip shows all 4 counted landing inside my 3 to 5 days, so I can see it is leaning my way but is not yet a call.
screens.why_b2: The days-out-of-7 axis and the median of 5 read at once, but the legend 'what you said at what you said beyond, the good side short of it' is garbled, and 'your bar · 3 of 4' with the marker at 3 takes a second look before I see it means 2 in 3 of the 4 counted.
screens.why_b3: 'Fall behind on their call reports on 3 to 5 days out of 7' is how I'd say it for my officers, but Frequency was not one of the two beliefs I checked on the way in, so the line is recognisably mine without being one I signed off on.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it does not say that one more counted officer would settle it, or that 4 of 4 inside my range means the lean is my way.
screens.why_b5: The low n is said plainly ('a small group: a lean, not a call'), but the header says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered · 4 counted', which made me stop and wonder who was dropped.
screens.instead: Leaning your way, not yet a call: all 4 officers counted fell behind on 3 to 5 days (middle answer 5); 6 answered, 2 not counted (one would rather not say, one guessed); one more counted answer settles it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know nothing is decided because one more counted officer was needed, though the verdict's '4 answered' should read '4 counted' since the count line says 6 answered.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes clear the bars count 8 picks from 4 people, but the strip is meant to show one cell per person and instead shows 8 cells (3 for, 5 against), and 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads as both the bar and my result, so I had to look twice to see 3 of 4 officers put reports in their two against a bar of 2 in 3.
screens.why_b3: The card says Importance and the belief line word for word as I checked it, and 'Writing up reports from body-cam footage' is my problem in my words.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that one more officer who names a real week would settle it, or that 3 of 4 is a lean above my bar.
screens.why_b5: The small n is stated and the lean is not called a result, but the strip's '5 against' makes it look as if five officers were against when only Kenji was, and the verdict's '4 answered' hides the 6 who did answer.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 officers counted put report writing in their two (bar 2 in 3), a lean your way; one more counted answer would settle it. 6 answered, Sean and Luis not counted.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the count line repeats why: Sean declined and Luis was a guess.
screens.why_b2: What is counted and over how many is plain, but 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads at first like my result rather than where 2 in 3 of 4 falls, and the ghost fifth cell in the strip takes a second look to understand.
screens.why_b3: The belief line is word for word the one I checked, and 'Current solution' is the dimension I confirmed under The Problem.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted officer would settle it, or that 3 of 4 already lean my way.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the low count is named ('a small group: a lean, not a call'), and 3 of 4 is not passed off as held.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 officers counted fell short of finishing at the desk, a lean your way, but you need one more counted answer to call it, so send the study to a few more patrol officers.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly which number keeps it open.
screens.why_b3: The line is named Importance and carries my belief word for word: five hard things in a week on patrol, with body-cam report writing in the two they'd most like made easier.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Code Four or what to do next, such as getting one more officer through Importance or whether Kenji's staffing point should change my pitch to chiefs; and the Current solution line I checked has no box and no note.
screens.why_b5: The count is plain ('1 against · 1 asked their why here', a group of 1), and the quote is shown as one officer's view, not as a theme across the force.
screens.why_b6: Kenji tells me something I didn't write: on a short-staffed shift, staffing and response times outrank paperwork, and simple reports already get done in the car between calls, so my pain may sit in the long reports, not every call.
screens.instead: Importance: too few to call, 4 of 5 needed, so get one more officer through. The one officer against puts staffing first and writes simple reports in the car, so test whether the pain is the long reports (DUIs, arrests). Current solution: say why it has no box here.

screens.why1: First screen and it checks whether my department is the size the study is about, so it's obvious why they ask before anything else.
screens.why2: I get it on one read, but I'd pause on whether they mean sworn officers or everybody on the payroll including dispatch and civilians, and a deputy might not call their sheriff's office a department with officers.
screens.why3: I know roughly how many sworn we have, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a size check, and no escape is needed on a gate.
screens.why5: It only asks about department size, nothing about any product or what they're selling.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and yes or no is easy to hold by ear; 'I'll read 2 options' is a bit stiff but says fine.
screens.instead: Does your department or sheriff's office have between 10 and 200 sworn officers or deputies? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After checking my department size, asking whether I fell behind on reports this week is the obvious next thing, because that is the whole subject.
screens.why2: I'd say 'reports' or 'incident reports', not 'call reports', and 'fall behind' is loose: behind the end of shift, behind the sergeant's deadline, or behind on approvals?
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I clocked out late or left a report for tomorrow this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chips don't fit: a gate should have no escape, 'I'd rather not say' isn't allowed, and 'I can't recall one particular call' doesn't answer a whole-week yes-or-no.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but 'fall behind' narrows the founder's point (turning a call's body-cam footage into an accurate report) to a backlog question, and the follow-up story about 'your last call' doesn't tie back to falling behind.
screens.why6: One short question ending 'Yes or no', easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you end a shift with a report still to write? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said yes to falling behind, so asking how often that week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: I'd say 'reports' or 'incident reports', not 'call reports', and on a 4-10 schedule 'days' is fuzzier to me than 'shifts', so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I only worked four or five shifts this week and a report I didn't finish rolls over to the next shift, so counting the days I was behind is partly a guess.
screens.why4: One through seven covers it, but 6 and 7 hardly fit someone on a shift rotation, and 'shifts' would have matched how I count my week.
screens.why5: It just asks about my reports in my week; nothing about a product or anyone's plan reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question and 'say a number from 1 to 7, or say you can't recall' is easy to hold and answer by ear.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many of your shifts did you leave a report unfinished at clock-out? (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or more; I can't recall)

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I fell behind on reports, asking which part of the week I'd most want made easier is a natural next step.
screens.why2: Court prep, short-staffed shifts, training hours and writing reports are all everyday words on patrol, and I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: Every option is something I dealt with this past week on patrol, so I can answer from my own shifts.
screens.why4: 'Getting to calls without a long wait' is odd because I don't wait to get to calls, dispatch and backlog do, and the report option alone carries a how-detail ('from body-cam footage') the others lack, so it stands out.
screens.why5: The report job is kept, but tacking 'from body-cam footage' onto only that option leans toward the founder's angle and hints at what's being sold.
screens.why6: One short question with five short parallel options and one escape said last; I can hold it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: Think of your last week on patrol. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Getting ready for court; keeping up with calls holding in the queue; covering shifts with too few officers; keeping up with required training; or writing up your call reports. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After asking how often I fell behind and what I'd want easier, asking how my last call's report actually got done is the natural next step.
screens.why2: I don't write up footage, I write the report from the call and check the footage, and 'across several tools' is not how I'd put it, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly when and where my last report got written, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: The five cover the real spread from the car to never, but the last one packs a second clause about reports piling up, and 'details fading' adds a judgement to a timing option.
screens.why5: 'Across several tools' slips in the founder's siloed-systems premise, which I never said and which isn't how every report I write goes.
screens.why6: The stem is about the right length, but 'writing up body-cam footage as a report across several tools' is a mouthful, and the last option, said with its semicolon as a comma, comes out as a sentence.
screens.instead: Think of your last call. When did its report get written? Written in the car between calls; finished at the desk before end of shift; stayed past end of shift to finish; left for the next shift; or still not written. Or say you can't recall.
